definition: Methodical means working through a task step by step, in a set order.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word methodical. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know methodical should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: His methodical weeding — one bed each morning, edges last, always — has left the garden nothing to hide.
An organized workshop has a place for everything; a methodical worker adds an order for every step of the doing.
Regimented goes past methodical — the steps are imposed like drill, allowing no judgment and no exceptions at all.

Structured says a thing is built to a clear plan — a structured essay, a structured argument — and describes the design of the thing itself. Methodical describes the doing: a person actually working through those steps in their set order, one after another, skipping none.

Disciplined is about self-control — sticking to the drill even when tired, tempted, or under pressure. Methodical is about order rather than willpower: the steps come in a fixed sequence and each waits its turn. A methodical worker on an easy day is still methodical; discipline only shows when it costs.

Methodical means working through a task step by step, in a set order.

A concert grand holds over two hundred strings, and Vasquez greets every one in the same methodical order: unisons first, then octaves, middle C outward, bass last, no matter how badly the treble jangles.
Impatient tuners chase whichever string sounds worst and end up chasing their own corrections around the piano all afternoon.
Vasquez finishes in three hours because the fixed order, not the ear alone, carries the work.
Methodical is the exact word because the tuning is done in an orderly, step-by-step way — the order is load-bearing.
Note what the word does not claim: not brilliance, not speed, not even fine detail, just a series of steps followed until the job closes behind you.
A methodical worker can be wrong; what they cannot be is lost.
Methodical praises the order of the doing — steps in their set order, nothing skipped.
It says nothing about fineness: for care poured into tiny details, use this unit's meticulous; for a bar nothing can clear, fastidious.
You can be methodical about coarse work — mucking stalls in the same brisk order every dawn — and the word fits perfectly.

Apprentices came to Etta Kwan expecting secrets about pianos.
What she taught instead was a sequence.
Her tuning was methodical to a degree that startled them: middle octave first, always; then fifths outward; then the extremes; the same order in a concert hall as in a kindergarten.
One apprentice, gifted and impatient, tried skipping to the problem keys.
The piano sounded worse each time, in new ways.
She reset to the middle octave and started the sequence over, letting the instrument make her argument.
Years later her apprentices disagreed about tools and brands, but every one of them tuned in her order, step after step, skipping nothing.
